items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Stanford team revives bleached corals through brief clone contact
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Stanford researchers report that bleached coral fragments fully recovered within seven weeks in laboratory tests after brief contact with healthy, genetically identical clones, according to a study published Oct. 14 in *Science Advances*. Contact lasting five days to a week was sometimes enough; bleached fragments kept a few millimeters away from healthy partners died. Microscopic channels in the corals’ tissues aligned, allowing beneficial algae to move between fragments within three days. Inside bleached fragments, algae populations doubled every four days during the second week. The method requires matching clones, limiting its use across reefs. The researchers plan to test other ways to deliver algae, including collecting it from healthy corals before heat waves.

items.title: [phys.org] Full-scale wave test shows salt marshes can buffer coastal storms
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers moved 306 square meters of intact salt marsh into the Delta Flume, a large wave-testing facility in Delft, Netherlands, and exposed it to waves as high as 2 meters. After 21 hours, the marsh surface had eroded by an average of just 7 millimeters, while its vegetation suffered progressive damage. The study found that plants can reduce wave energy by more than 10%, and by as much as 50% on lower-energy coasts with waves up to 1 meter. Their effect declines as waves grow higher and vegetation is lost. Researchers say marshes could work alongside dikes and seawalls, not replace them. A Spanish coastal-engineering expert questioned how well the Dutch experiment applies to other coastlines, citing wave periods and mobile seabeds among other factors.

items.title: [thehackernews.com] Attackers compromise AI gateway LiteLLM 1.107.0 to steal credentials
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Attackers released a malicious version of LiteLLM, an open-source gateway for connecting to AI models, distributing version 1.107.0 through the Python Package Index (PyPI) and Docker images on Oct. 21. The package installed a credential stealer and a backdoor that could collect cloud and AI service keys, private keys, browser data and other secrets. The code could run whenever Python started, even in programs that did not use LiteLLM. LiteLLM said attackers used three engineers’ GitHub credentials to alter and approve the release, but it has not identified how they obtained those credentials. PyPI removed the package, and affected Docker image tags were removed or replaced. The company advised users to rebuild from a clean environment, rotate exposed credentials and use version 1.106.2 while the investigation continues.

items.title: [dw.com] AI-discovered PHP flaws prompt global website shutdowns as patches roll out
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

PHP’s maintainers released fixes on Oct. 21 for two critical vulnerabilities that could let attackers run code on exposed web servers without logging in, prompting governments and companies to take websites offline while they applied patches. The flaws, rated 9.2 out of 10, affect PHP installations serving web requests; the PHP team released patched versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. Precautionary shutdowns affected public services and businesses in Europe, Australia and Asia. France disabled local-government sites, the Netherlands took its DigiD digital identity portal and parliamentary sites offline, and Japanese companies suspended some online services; Wikipedia’s operator also temporarily took supporting systems offline. PHP underpins an estimated 70% of websites, though only sites running PHP on their own servers are exposed. Researchers at Calif and Wiz found the flaws using AI tools in August, and details leaked online on Oct. 20, a day before the planned patch release. Cloudflare reported millions of exploitation attempts after disclosure, while Amazon said it detected an attempt against a decoy system on Oct. 17; reports described attempts but no confirmed successful exploitation at that point. Agencies advised organizations to patch promptly or isolate vulnerable systems until they could apply the fixes.

items.title: [Fast Company] AI fear is driving employees to slack off, show up late, and even steal coworkers’ lunches
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

As more businesses adopt artificial intelligence, some employees—who are increasingly worried about losing their jobs—are starting to act out.

That’s the finding of a new study from Washington State University researchers, published in the journal Occupational Health Science, that looks at how AI adoption at work is affecting workers’ attitudes and behaviors in the office.

Research has shown that the increase of AI-based technologies at work—such as intelligent robotics, automated systems, and algorithmic management—may make employees feel insecure about their jobs and lead to more stress and less engagement.

Washington State University’s study looked at employees across 18 different industries and found that workers who had the greatest fears about being replaced by AI were more likely to behave poorly by, for example, slacking off at the office or even stealing a coworker’s lunch.

Researchers also found that employees who assumed they would be displaced were more likely to “morally disengage” at work, such as by coming in late for a shift or surfing the web while on the clock.

“Moral disengagement is basically a way of justifying bad behavior,” Tahira M. Probst, a professor of psychology at WSU Vancouver and lead author of the study, said in a news release. “We know what’s right and wrong. We know what organizational policies say we can and can’t do. Moral disengagement is a way of reframing that behavior as something that is acceptable.”

Researchers used the AI Industry Exposure index to identify which industries were most exposed to potential AI disruption. Workers in finance and insurance had some of the highest levels of exposure, while workers in agriculture, forestry, and construction had the least. Not surprisingly, the bad behavior was more pronounced in the industries with the highest amount of disruption.

The study’s bottom line: When employees feel their jobs are at risk, they may look at workplace expectations differently and rationalize behaviors such as cutting corners or undermining coworkers to protect themselves or compensate for what they perceive as injustice.

The findings also suggest that AI anxieties can hurt workers and businesses alike, pointing to the need for employers to be more mindful of how they roll out AI in the workplace so employees are better supported.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Sam Buchanan, Druv Pai, Peng Wang, Yi Ma, GitHub, Oct 22, 2026

This is "a modern fully open-source textbook exploring why and how deep neural networks learn compact and information-dense representations of high-dimensional real-world data." It's a daunting read - and to be honest, I gave the first chapter a careful read but have only skimmed the rest (though it's now on my virtual bookshelf for future reference). I think people who are serious about understanding how we learn and how machines emulate this should at the very least read that first chapter. It contains what is to my understanding an accurate history of artificial intelligence (including the important early work in computation, cybernetics, and information theory). The aim of the book is to give us a framework that explains how neural networks work to generate intelligence. They authors write, "intelligence is not about collecting all informative data in advance and training a model to memorize their (low-dimensional) distribution. Instead, it requires computational mechanisms that can continuously improve current knowledge of the distribution and acquire new information when needed. A fundamental characteristic of any intelligent being or system - whether an animal, a human, a civilization, or the entire scientific community - is the ability to continuously improve or gain new information or knowledge on its own."

items.title: [koaa.com] U.S. emissions rise worsens global warming outlook, UN report says
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 emissions assessment says U.S. greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 133 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2025, the largest increase among major economies. The United States accounted for about 70% of the net increase among 124 countries whose emissions grew. The report warns that the world can no longer avoid exceeding the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C threshold and must limit the overshoot. The U.S. increase reflected higher electricity demand and a rebound in coal-fired power generation, while global greenhouse-gas emissions remained roughly level at 58.4 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. The assessment attributes its worsening projections partly to the United States’ formal withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions. Under existing policies, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; fully meeting national climate pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. The next UN climate summit, COP31, is scheduled to open in Antalya, Türkiye, next month.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap Report says governments must now limit the scale and duration of global warming beyond 1.5°C, rather than try to prevent that threshold from being crossed. Its lowest-overshoot pathway would cap warming at 1.7°C to 1.8°C around mid-century, with about a 50% chance of returning to 1.5°C by 2100. Following that pathway requires greenhouse-gas emissions to fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, compared with 2025. If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; full delivery of pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. The pathway also calls for sharply reducing coal-fired electricity generation and scaling up carbon removal. The report warns that the required reductions are far beyond current plans. Governments are due to discuss climate action at the COP31 summit, scheduled to open in Antalya on Nov. 9.

Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed in principle to resume U.S.-mediated talks with Ukraine after Nov. 10, following a nearly three-hour meeting on Oct. 21 with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. Kremlin foreign-policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said the technical-level negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi and focus on a postwar security framework for Russia and Ukraine. A technical-level meeting is the next step, but no firm date or venue has been announced. The Kremlin said talks could begin after Nov. 10.

items.title: [scimex.org] UN warns record El Niño could disrupt weather into 2027
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, warned Oct. 21 that the developing El Niño could push sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific to 3.8°C above average from November through January, with a peak around December. The agency said that level would exceed anything in its four decades of monitoring records. El Niño can shift global rainfall patterns, bringing drought to some areas and heavy rain, floods and heat to others. The WMO expects risks across Latin America, eastern and southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific. Extreme weather has already been reported and could compound humanitarian emergencies. UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said about 50 million people could face increased hunger. He said he had released $50 million for 11 countries and called on governments and development finance institutions to fund preparations before damage occurs. The event is forecast to peak late in 2026, but its effects may persist into 2027 and beyond. Scientists say regional consequences vary: El Niño is a natural climate pattern, but its interaction with human-caused warming and other ocean conditions can influence its effects. Forecasts cannot reliably predict individual storms months in advance.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Companies and governments are adopting AI agents that can carry out tasks, while researchers and policymakers examine their effects on jobs, security and investment. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said he uses agents to summarize internal discussions and track computing use, but humans still make consequential decisions about allocating resources. Google has also introduced agentic AI for public agencies, and the United Arab Emirates plans to shift half of federal government operations and services to autonomous agents within two years. Stanford University researchers report that employment in AI-exposed software development and customer-service jobs fell by more than 4% this year, while Harvard researchers say current labor-market signals offer little certainty about AI’s longer-term effects. Central bankers are assessing potential effects on wages and productivity, and a University of Hawaiʻi analysis estimates that AI investment and related stock gains have supported U.S. growth and consumer spending. Security teams report difficulty verifying agents’ answers, and AI infrastructure borrowers, including CoreWeave, face rising credit risks. Center for Internet Security senior director of threat intelligence TJ Sayers said autonomous AI attacks are no longer hypothetical. Agent use remained in single digits across almost every business function, according to the Stanford 2026 AI Index cited by The National.

items.title: [agrifocusafrica.com] Uganda targets 10,000 tractors in five-year mechanization push
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Uganda plans to deploy 10,000 tractors over five years to expand mechanized farming, Agriculture Minister Frank Tumwebaze told Parliament on Oct. 21. The strategy proposes 21 mechanization centers and a cost-sharing model involving the government, commercial farmers and producer groups. Tumwebaze said dependence on manual labor and unpredictable weather constrain productivity, while machinery could help farmers cultivate more land and support value-added production. Kubota and autonomy-software company Agtonomy are extending a pilot to automate orchard work such as spraying, mowing and underplant cultivation. In the United States, drone-treated acreage grew to 16.4 million acres in 2025. Equipment makers have also introduced higher-capacity grain conveyors designed to reduce harvest handling time.
